newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Japan join in verbal move to prop up yen.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Japan join in verbal move to prop up yen.

text.p: The United States joined Japan on Thursday in a verbal effort to prop up a sliding yen that threatens to spark new trade tensions between the two countries.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin backed concerns expressed by Japanese finance officials that the yen's recent fall against the dollar had been excessive and that Japan would deal decisively with any such excessive moves.
"We share the concern expressed by the Japanese authorities last night about recent movements in the yen because of the impact on Japan's external (trade) surplus," Rubin said.

Rubin went out of his way to make clear his support for the Japanese comments. He discussed U.S. currency policy both in a telephone conference to reporters who had travelled with him to Asia and in an interview with CNBC business television.

But currency traders greeted the comments with some scepticism. At midday, after Rubin had made his remarks, the dollar edged higher to 1.7182 German marks and 125.93 Japanese yen from 1.7155 and 125.75 at the opening. But it later fell to 125.85 yen and 1.7190 marks by the close of trading, from 126.80 yen and 1.7255 marks on Wednesday.

"If Rubin doesn't say what he's going to do about it, it doesn't really matter. The market is focused on the fact that he hasn't changed his dollar policy," said Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd.
Rubin, in his comments to reporters and CNBC, said U.S. policy on the dollar has not changed and that it is in the country's interest to have a strong currency.

"They want to stabilise the situation, but the market hasn't really paid much attention," said David Gilmore, partner in Foreign Exchange Analytics. "In order to impress currency traders, Treasury is going to have to sell some dollars."
The last time the Treasury intervened in currency markets was in the third quarter of 1995.
A weak yen makes Japanese products cheaper in global markets, while the strong dollar is making U.S. goods less competitive.

U.S. manufacturers, particularly carmakers, who see Japanese companies grabbing a bigger share of the domestic market, have voiced their worries about the impact of a weak yen and strong dollar on their businesses.

U.S. officials have also expressed concern about Japan's rising trade surplus and have said several times in recent weeks that Japan should not try to export its way out of sluggish growth. Rubin spoke with Japanese officials about U.S. concerns during a visit to Tokyo last Friday.
But since that meeting. the dollar has strenthened, hitting a 4-1/2-year high of 127 yen to a dollar Wednesday.
Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told bank executives Thursday that the yen's recent weakness against the dollar had been excessive.
"We will act decisively in a timely manner when exchange rates move excessively," he said in a speech. "The recent movement of the yen is obviously excessive, and I am concerned about it."

Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara said in an interview in Japan that intervention in foreign exchange markets was possible if exchange rates deviated greatly from fundamental economic conditions. He added that he did not think recent currency movements were in line with those conditions.
